candidates.label: B073poison (counter-code, test case)
candidates.change: Counter, not a candidate. Starts from B051 cMovsw (rev0 MOVSW twin: mov al,0A2h -> 0A3h). Its own hook cell is moved 4A17h -> 7B2Dh in A and B, so it shares no cell with rev0. B's 5th instruction mov [5D13h],bx becomes mov [4A17h],bx. rev0 B writes [4A17h] once, at instr 3. The counter overwrites it at instr 5, before any hooked Zombie reads it (zom20a is hooked at A instr 10, b/d at B instr 12). Every Zombie that rev0 hooks then jumps into the counter's zombie_entry. Control B073ctl is the same code with the [5D13h] write kept (2 bytes differ in B; A is identical).
candidates.groupNotes: Control: agent2/night/scratch/B073/ctlA.asm and ctlB.asm (B sha 755cac3f..., A same as the counter). Base (rev0) team score, 12 cohorts x 20 battles each, filled with 2025 teams and the zom20 pack. Copies 1 (9xz3y): vs ctl 0.266 (SE 0.032), vs poison 0.201 (SE 0.029); base B member 0.173 -> 0.071; counter team 0.467 -> 0.633. Copies 2 (wu55u): vs ctl 0.137 (SE 0.025), vs poison 0.091 (SE 0.010). Copies 3 (d05lf): vs ctl 0.056, vs poison 0.062 (at the floor). The base-vs-ctl/poison comparison is unpaired (different fill teams). The paired evidence is the relocation arm below.

candidates.label: reloc (B053 reloc-hook-B6E9, re-used as defense arm)
candidates.change: A and B: every use of the cell 4A17h is replaced by 0B6E9h (B053 binaries, unchanged). The cell is no longer shared, but it is still fixed and guessable.
candidates.groupNotes: Paired against the base on the poisoner: copies 1 (9xz3y) +0.0958 [0.0434,0.1483] W/L 9/3, vs ctl +0.0063 [-0.006,0.0185]; copies 2 (wu55u) +0.0465 [0.0292,0.0639] 11/0, vs ctl -0.0021; copies 3 (d05lf) +0.0052 [-0.0021,0.0125] (floor), vs ctl -0.0021. General: B053 screen uunhx +0.0024. The protection holds only by construction: a counter that writes [0B6E9h] instead brings the damage back. This moves the exposure; it does not remove it.

candidates.label: bodycell (hook cells inside own bodies)
candidates.change: A: after mov [9769h],ax, add mov [si+cellA],ax (B's entry, read from [4A17h] at instr 4). INT87 uses lea cx,[si+cellA] instead of mov cx,4A17h, so zom20a becomes jmp [cellA]. cellA is a dw at the end of A. B: add mov [si+cellB],bx before its INT87 and use lea cx,[si+cellB]. After cld, B self-patches the mov cx,4A17h immediate in zombie_entry to cellB (mov [si+zcx+1],cx). B still writes [4A17h] at instr 3, but only as the channel to A. Timing: A's INT87 moves to instr 11 (was 10), B's to instr 13 (was 12), and B reaches its phoenix 2 turns later.
candidates.screenJob: none (no general screen; the 4-job budget was used)
candidates.groupNotes: Threat j77yv (same cohorts as 9xz3y, copies 1): ALL +0.1063 [0.0632,0.1493] 20/0; poison +0.1507 [0.0788,0.2226] 10/0 (base 0.201 -> 0.352); ctl +0.0618 [0.0273,0.0963] 10/0 (0.266 -> 0.328). The theft-specific part (poison minus ctl) is about +0.089, the same as reloc (+0.090). The extra +0.06 against the plain MOVSW twin is probably a timing effect: the twin runs in lockstep with rev0, and the 1-2 turn shift breaks that. General cost is unknown. Earlier waves found that timing shifts in B's startup and zombie path are chaotic on the 2025 field.

threatFindings.threat: When the fixed cells are read. [4A17h] is written once, by B at instr 3. A reads it at instr 4 and copies it to [9769h]. B's phoenix_init also reads it, but and dx,0 / or dx,0FFBh throws the value away. Each hooked Zombie (FF 26 17 4A) reads it once, on its first pass through the patched jmp: zom20a after A's INT87 at instr 10, b/d after B's INT87 at instr 12 and after each later INT87 in zombie_entry. Neither our code nor our Zombies ever read [5D13h] or [9769h]; those cells only matter for stealing other teams' Zombies.
threatFindings.evidence: Static reading of rev0 A.asm/B.asm and of int87() in Cpu.java (it does not change registers). Confirmed by the poisoner: one write at instr 5 is enough to take over all hooked Zombies (jobs 9xz3y, wu55u).
threatFindings.impact: The theft window runs from round 4 until the first Zombie read (about round 11 or later). Any write in that window redirects the Zombies.

threatFindings.threat: A purpose-built [4A17h] poisoner (one mov [4A17h],bx at instr 5) redirects all of the base's captured Zombies into its own code.
threatFindings.evidence: 9xz3y (copies 1): relocated-cell arm vs base, paired on the same cohorts: poison +0.096 [0.043,0.148] 9/3, ctl +0.006. Unpaired: base 0.266 vs ctl and 0.201 vs poison. Base B member 0.173 -> 0.071. Poisoner team 0.633 vs ctl 0.467. wu55u (copies 2): paired +0.047 [0.029,0.064] 11/0; base 0.137 -> 0.091.
threatFindings.impact: About -0.065 to -0.1 per battle for the base against one poisoner, and about -0.05 against two. The stolen Zombies run the counter's MOVSW phoenix, which mostly kills B. Today the only realistic writers of this cell are the V6 family, which write at the same instr 3 (B053/B063; A003 measured +0.015).

threatFindings.evidence: d05lf: paired +0.005 [-0.002,0.013]; the base scores about 0.06 against both ctl and poison.
threatFindings.impact: Three MOVSW twins already push the base to the floor, so the theft adds nothing measurable there.

threatFindings.threat: Hook cells inside our own bodies (bodycell) remove the fixed-cell theft.
threatFindings.evidence: j77yv: poison +0.151 [0.079,0.223] 10/0, ctl +0.062 [0.027,0.096] 10/0, so the theft-specific gain is about +0.089 (reloc: +0.090).
threatFindings.impact: Protects against any fixed-cell poisoner. The general field cost was not measured.

threatFindings.threat: Remaining exposure of bodycell: A still learns B's entry through [4A17h] (B writes it in round 3, A reads it in round 4). A poisoner that writes in a loop, or one that follows the pointer, could still win that 1-round window. A channel through team-shared memory would close it, but it needs DS switching because segment prefixes are invalid.
threatFindings.evidence: Static only; no looping poisoner was built.
threatFindings.impact: Only A's zom20a path is affected; the b/d hooks use cellB directly.

threatFindings.threat: A write to [5D13h] or [9769h] redirects our own Zombies.
threatFindings.evidence: Static: our hooks only use CX=4A17h (B053, B063). The poisoner leaves these cells alone and still takes everything through 4A17h.

recommendation: Do not promote anything from B073. The poisoner (agent2/night/scratch/B073/counterA.asm and counterB.asm, control ctlA/ctlB) is a clean 2-byte test case for domain 3: it takes about 0.07-0.1 per battle from rev0 at 1 copy and about 0.05 at 2 copies. Moving the cell to another fixed address (B053 reloc) beats it only by construction. bodycell (bcA/bcB, A 201 B, B 213 B) is the principled fix and clearly blocks the theft (+0.151 vs the poisoner, 10/0). Its general cost has not been measured, though, and it shifts startup timing by 1-2 turns, which has been chaotic on the 2025 field. Next step for whoever continues: screen bodycell. If it is neutral, keep it as a robustness add-on in a combination, and add the poisoner to the threat library.
